Reprimand

REP-rih-mand -- from Latin reprimere, 're- (back) + premere (to press)': to reprimand is to 'press back' against bad behavior with an official scolding. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To reprimand to officially scold or admonish someone for a fault or a mistake.

The principal called both boys into her office to reprimand them for the fight in the cafeteria.

Worked Example

After the intern forwarded a confidential email to the wrong client, her manager reprimanded her privately in his office rather than in front of the whole team.

Reprimand always involves someone in authority delivering an official, targeted scolding for a specific fault -- notice that the manager, not a coworker, is the one doing the reprimanding, and the mistake is specific and real.

How Reprimand Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

scold

scold: to criticize someone sharply for doing something wrong

admonish

admonish: to warn or correct someone firmly but respectfully

Antonyms

praise

praise: to express approval or admiration

commend

commend: to officially praise someone's actions

How Strong Is It? — scold → reprimand → censure

scold vs. reprimand

scold vs. reprimand: Scold is the milder, everyday word -- a parent scolds a child for tracking mud inside, while to reprimand someone carries more weight because the criticism comes officially, from a boss or a principal, for a real fault.

censure vs. reprimand

censure vs. reprimand: Censure goes further than reprimand: a reprimand might happen quietly in an office, but a censure is a severe, formal condemnation, often voted on the record for everyone to see.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back, again (Latin)

Root — prim

Root — prim: to press (from Latin premere, 'to press' -- the same root that appears as -press- in suppress)

Suffix — -and

Suffix — -and: the tail end of the Latin gerundive ending -enda, 'that which is to be...' (as in reprimenda culpa, 'a fault to be checked')

Put it together

Put it together: Reprimand traces to Latin reprimenda (culpa), 'a fault to be pressed back': re- ('back') + prim (from premere, 'to press') + -and (the worn-down end of that Latin ending). To reprimand someone is literally to 'press back' against their bad behavior with an official scolding.

Use the root in a new word: suppress

Use the root in a new word: suppress: The librarian moved quickly to suppress the rumor before it spread through the whole school.

Word Choice

Reprimand can also be a noun for the scolding itself (a formal reprimand went into his file), but this unit teaches the verb sense. It differs from the milder, more personal Reproach and the more formal, often public Censure -- all three appear in this unit.
